newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols off highs but well bid.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt vols off highs but well bid.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. debt options were off highs but stayed well bid as the underlying markets whipsawed, turning down sharply after an early rally and then clawing back up, traders said.
"The market moved around a lot, obviously," a Treasury bond options trader at the Chicago Board of Trade said. "There were a lot of things trading, but generally volatilities were pumped up."
Implied volatility for December T-bond futures options rose about 0.2 point to 8.8 percent.
Volatility for September options, which expire in just over a week and tend to swing around a lot, stood at 9.6 percent, slightly off on the day as futures recovered losses in the afternoon.

But traders noted that the volatility curve was still inverted due to demand for gamma, reflecting the wild gyrations in the underlying market and nervousness over inflation. Shorter-dated options are rich in gamma, which provides them with quicker premium acceleration and bigger delta changes.
The August 19 Federal Open Market Committee meeting added to the risk premium on the September contracts, which expire on August 22.

T-bond futures ended slightly firmer after a hectic, wide-ranging session. They dived through support levels to a low of 111-31/32 in mid-morning after an early spike up to a high of 113-19/32 triggered by favorable economic data.

The July U.S. producer price index fell 0.1 percent in both the overall and the core rates, against average estimates of a 0.1 point rise in both. July retail sales gained 0.6 percent overall versus forecasts for a 0.7 percent gain.
At the shorter end of the curve, Eurodollar volatilities were also bid up during the mid-morning selloff in futures before drifting back lower as futures recovered.
Implied volatilities for December and March Eurodollar futures options stood at around 8.8 and 10.8 percent respectively, little changed on the day.
A brokerage firm trader said mid-curve options, which are priced off of 1998 futures but expire in the coming months, continued to attract strong interest because of their relatively high gamma.
